headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage via shared Replit workspace plus Semantic Kernel MCP/plugin pathways; defaults also create cascading trust and capability conflicts.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A writes and reads Repl workspace files by default, while agent B reads/writes application-defined files and can use MCP servers/plugins. That creates a plausible shared-content bridge where A’s outputs can be consumed by B as instructions. The pathway is not proven to be isolated, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent A writes attacker-controlled text into a shared workspace file that agent B later reads as prompt material
IF agent B’s plugin or MCP layer forwards file content into tool instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces so A and B never read the same files
Add a provenance tag to every file B ingests
Disable automatic prompt construction from workspace files
Require manual review before B consumes A-generated artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches secrets and deployment configuration and has broad network egress; agent B can call Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face and MCP servers. If they share workspace data, A’s secrets or config can flow into B’s outbound API calls. Because both profiles expose write/read file surfaces and B’s egress is broad, the leakage path is credible in default setups.
conditions: IF agent A stores secrets or deployment config in the Repl workspace
IF agent B sends workspace contents to a third-party model or MCP server
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared files and use isolated secret stores
Block B from reading A’s workspace directories
Restrict B’s outbound providers to a vetted allowlist
Redact secrets before any B-side tool call
Rotate any credentials that may already have been exposed

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can execute shell commands, modify git state, and write the Repl filesystem; agent B can also read/write files and use MCP-backed tools. With no locking or coordination primitive documented between them, concurrent writes to shared mutable resources can corrupt state or overwrite each other. The overlap is broad enough to treat as high risk.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace path
IF either agent modifies git state while the other writes files concurrently
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent
Serialize git operations through one operator-controlled queue
Disable concurrent writes during shared tasks
Use branch-per-agent workflows with explicit merge review
Add file locks for any shared mutable resource

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B is an orchestration layer that can treat upstream outputs as inputs to plugins or model calls, while agent A produces code and workspace artifacts. That makes it plausible for B to act on A’s output without verification. The pair does not prove automatic execution, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text or files as authoritative task context
IF B triggers downstream tool calls based on A’s output without a validation step
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B acts on A’s output
Require schema validation for A-produced artifacts
Have B cite source files before executing actions
Limit B to read-only review until outputs are checked

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A explicitly handles secrets and deployment configuration in a Replit cloud workspace, while agent B routes data to external model providers and MCP servers. Even without a named residency mismatch, the differing retention and processing surfaces create a plausible compliance gap for sensitive code or secrets. The evidence is profile-only, so I avoid stronger claims.
conditions: IF regulated or customer-sensitive data is placed into the shared workspace
IF B forwards that data to a third-party model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s shared context
Document a data-processing agreement for every external provider
Disable logging for sensitive prompts and outputs
Use separate tenants or projects for regulated workloads
